topics.name: Temperature Scales and Thermal Expansion of Solids, Liquids, and Gases
topics.summary: Temperature measures how hot a body is and is read on three common scales. The Celsius scale puts the ice point at 0 °C and the steam point at 100 °C; the Fahrenheit scale puts them at 32 °F and 212 °F; the Kelvin scale starts at absolute zero, so 0 °C is 273 K. An absolute reading converts with both a scale factor and an offset, but a temperature change uses only the scale factor, because the offset cancels when two readings are subtracted. Most solids expand on heating. A length grows by a fraction \( \alpha\Delta T \), an area by \( \beta\Delta T \) and a volume by \( \gamma\Delta T \), where for an isotropic solid \( \beta=2\alpha \) and \( \gamma=3\alpha \). Liquids have only volume expansion, and a container's own expansion hides part of it. An ideal gas at constant pressure has \( \gamma=\dfrac{1}{T} \) with T in kelvin. Water is unusual: it contracts between 0 °C and 4 °C and is densest at 4 °C. Uneven expansion bends bimetallic strips, and a clamped rod develops thermal stress.
key_formulas: \( \Delta L=L_0\alpha\Delta T \), \( \Delta A=A_0\beta\Delta T \), \( \Delta V=V_0\gamma\Delta T \)
topics.worked_example:
A brass plate (\( \alpha=2\times10^{-5} \) per °C) of area \( 0.5\text{ m}^2 \) is heated from 20 °C to 70 °C. Find the increase in area.

\( \beta=2\alpha=4\times10^{-5} \) per °C and \( \Delta T=50 \) °C.

\( \Delta A=0.5\times4\times10^{-5}\times50=1\times10^{-3}\text{ m}^2 \).
common_mistakes: Adding \( +32 \) or \( +273 \) when converting a temperature change instead of a reading
Leaving out the offset when converting an absolute reading
Swapping the ratios, e.g. \( \beta=3\alpha \) or \( \gamma=2\alpha \)
Using the linear formula \( \Delta L=L_0\alpha\Delta T \) for an area or volume change
Thinking a hole in a heated plate shrinks

topics.name: Calorimetry: Specific Heat Capacity and the Principle of Calorimetry
topics.summary: When heat flows into a body without a change of state, its temperature rises by an amount set by its mass and specific heat capacity: \( Q=mc\Delta T \). Specific heat c is the heat needed to warm 1 kg by 1 K; water's large value, 4200 J/(kg·K) or 1 cal/(g·°C), makes it an excellent coolant and moderates coastal climates. The heat capacity of a whole body is \( mc \), and the water equivalent of a calorimeter is the mass of water with the same heat capacity. The principle of calorimetry is energy conservation for an isolated system: total heat lost by hotter bodies equals total heat gained by colder ones, and all reach a common final temperature. To solve a mixture problem, write each body's heat term from its own starting temperature to the common final temperature, include the calorimeter, and balance lost against gained. Only temperature changes appear, so kelvin and Celsius give identical results. With a heater of power P and no losses, \( Pt=mc\Delta T \), which links time, power and temperature rise.
topics.worked_example:
0.5 kg of water at 90 °C is mixed with 1 kg of water at 30 °C. Find the final temperature.

\( 0.5c(90-T)=1\times c(T-30) \).

\( 45-0.5T=T-30 \), so \( 1.5T=75 \) and \( T=50 \) °C.
common_mistakes: Taking a simple average when masses or specific heats differ
Forgetting the heat absorbed by the calorimeter or container
Using an absolute temperature in place of \( \Delta T \)
Measuring each body's change from the wrong starting temperature
Leaving heat per minute unconverted when finding power in watts

topics.name: Change of State: Latent Heat and Phase Changes
topics.summary: Matter changes state when enough heat is added or removed: melting (fusion), freezing, vaporization, condensation and sublimation. During a change of state at fixed pressure the temperature stays constant, because the heat breaks or forms bonds instead of raising the average kinetic energy. The heat involved is \( Q=mL \), where L is the latent heat: for water, fusion needs about \( 3.36\times10^{5} \) J/kg (80 cal/g) and vaporization about \( 2.26\times10^{6} \) J/kg (540 cal/g). A heating curve therefore shows sloping parts, where one phase warms with \( Q=mc\Delta T \) using that phase's own specific heat, and flat parts, where latent heat is absorbed. Whenever a temperature range crosses a phase boundary, the total heat is a chain of separate terms: warm each phase, and add a latent term for each transition. Boiling point rises with pressure, as in a pressure cooker, and falls at altitude; pressure lowers ice's melting point, which explains regelation. Steam burns are severe because condensing steam releases its large latent heat.
key_formulas: Ice to steam: \( Q=mc_{ice}\Delta T_1+mL_f+mc_w\Delta T_2+mL_v+\dots \)
topics.worked_example:
Find the heat to turn 20 g of ice at 0 °C into water at 50 °C (\( L_f=80 \) cal/g, \( c_w=1 \) cal/(g·°C)).

Melt: \( 20\times80=1600 \) cal.

Warm: \( 20\times1\times50=1000 \) cal.

Total = 2600 cal.
common_mistakes: Skipping the \( mL \) term when the temperature range crosses a phase boundary
Applying one \( mc\Delta T \) across the whole range, or using water's specific heat for ice
Assuming all the ice melts without checking the available heat
Forgetting that condensed steam also cools after condensing
Confusing latent heat of fusion with latent heat of vaporization

topics.name: Heat Transfer by Conduction and Convection
topics.summary: Conduction carries heat through a material from hotter to colder regions without bulk movement; metals conduct well because free electrons carry energy. In steady state the heat current through a slab is \( H=\dfrac{kA\Delta T}{L} \), where k is the thermal conductivity in W/(m·K). It is useful to define thermal resistance \( R=\dfrac{L}{kA} \), so that \( H=\dfrac{\Delta T}{R} \), just like current in a circuit. Slabs in series carry the same heat current and their resistances add; the temperature drop across each slab is proportional to its resistance, which gives junction temperatures. Rods in parallel share the same temperature difference and their conductances add, so heat splits in proportion to kA/L. Still air, wool, thermocol and ice are poor conductors used for insulation. Convection transfers heat by the bulk movement of a fluid: warm fluid expands, becomes less dense and rises while cooler fluid sinks. It explains sea and land breezes, room heating from floor-level heaters, and why convection cannot occur in solids.
topics.worked_example:
A glass pane 4 mm thick, area \( 2\text{ m}^2 \), k = 0.8 W/(m·K), has faces at 25 °C and 5 °C. Find the heat flow.

\( H=\dfrac{0.8\times2\times20}{0.004} \).

\( H=8000 \) W.
common_mistakes: Leaving thickness in cm or mm instead of metres
Using the series formula for parallel rods, or the reverse
Splitting the temperature drop equally across unequal slabs
Putting the larger temperature drop across the better conductor
Treating convection as possible in a solid

topics.name: Heat Transfer by Radiation: Stefan's Law, Wien's Law, and Newton's Law of Cooling
topics.summary: Radiation carries heat as electromagnetic waves and needs no medium, which is how the Sun warms the Earth. A perfect black body absorbs all radiation falling on it and is also the best emitter; good absorbers are good emitters. Stefan's law gives the power radiated per unit area as \( E=e\sigma T^4 \), with \( \sigma=5.67\times10^{-8}\text{ W m}^{-2}\text{ K}^{-4} \), emissivity e (1 for a black body) and T the absolute temperature in kelvin. A body in surroundings at \( T_0 \) loses net power \( e\sigma A(T^4-T_0^4) \). Wien's displacement law, \( \lambda_{max}T=b \) with \( b=2.9\times10^{-3} \) m·K, says hotter bodies peak at shorter wavelengths, so blue stars are hotter than red ones. Newton's law of cooling states that the rate of cooling is proportional to the excess temperature over the surroundings. It is a linear approximation of the fourth-power law, valid only for small excesses, and is often applied using the average temperature over an interval.
topics.worked_example:
A black body at 127 °C is heated to 527 °C. By what factor does its radiated power increase?

In kelvin: 400 K and 800 K, a ratio of 2.

\( \dfrac{P_2}{P_1}=2^4=16 \).
common_mistakes: Substituting Celsius values into \( T^4 \) or \( \lambda_{max}T=b \)
Using \( T^2 \) or \( T^3 \) instead of \( T^4 \)
Thinking \( \lambda_{max} \) increases with temperature
Applying Newton's law of cooling to large temperature differences
Measuring the excess from 0 °C instead of from the surroundings

questions.topic: Temperature Scales and Thermal Expansion of Solids, Liquids, and Gases
questions.question: Convert a reading of 25 °C to the Kelvin scale.
questions.explanation:
An absolute Celsius reading converts to Kelvin by adding the zero-point offset: \( T_K=T_C+273 \).

\( T_K=25+273=298 \) K.
questions.hint: A reading (not a change) needs the zero-point offset.
distractor_logic: Subtracted 273 instead of adding it when converting a Celsius reading to Kelvin
Used the Fahrenheit formula \( \dfrac{9}{5}C+32 \) instead of the Kelvin offset
Treated an absolute reading like a temperature difference and dropped the \( +273 \) offset

questions.topic: Temperature Scales and Thermal Expansion of Solids, Liquids, and Gases
questions.question: The temperature of a liquid rises by 45 °C. What is this rise expressed on the Fahrenheit scale?
questions.explanation:
A temperature change converts using only the scale factor: \( \Delta T_F=\dfrac{9}{5}\Delta T_C \).

\( \Delta T_F=\dfrac{9}{5}\times45=81 \) °F.

No \( +32 \) is added, because the offset cancels when one reading is subtracted from another.
questions.hint: Is this a reading or a change? Changes use only the size of the degree.
distractor_logic: Added the \( +32 \) offset, which belongs only to absolute readings, not to a temperature change
Multiplied by \( \dfrac{5}{9} \) instead of \( \dfrac{9}{5} \)
Assumed a Celsius degree and a Fahrenheit degree are the same size

questions.topic: Temperature Scales and Thermal Expansion of Solids, Liquids, and Gases
questions.question: At what temperature do the Celsius and Fahrenheit scales show the same numerical reading?
questions.explanation:
Set \( F=C=x \) in \( F=\dfrac{9}{5}C+32 \): \( x=\dfrac{9}{5}x+32 \).

\( -\dfrac{4}{5}x=32 \), so \( x=-40 \).

Hence \( -40 \) °C and \( -40 \) °F are the same temperature.
questions.hint: Put F = C = x into the conversion formula and solve.
distractor_logic: Assumed both scales share the same zero point
Made a sign error while solving \( x=\dfrac{9}{5}x+32 \)
Confused the crossover point with absolute zero on the Celsius scale

questions.topic: Temperature Scales and Thermal Expansion of Solids, Liquids, and Gases
questions.question: A steel rod 2 m long is heated through 50 °C. If \( \alpha=1.2\times10^{-5} \) per °C, what is the increase in its length?
questions.explanation:
Linear expansion: \( \Delta L=L_0\alpha\Delta T \).

\( \Delta L=2\times1.2\times10^{-5}\times50=1.2\times10^{-3} \) m.

That is \( 1.2 \) mm.
questions.hint: For a length change, use the linear coefficient directly.
distractor_logic: Used the areal coefficient \( \beta=2\alpha \) for a change in length
Used the volume coefficient \( \gamma=3\alpha \) for a change in length
Computed only \( \alpha\Delta T \) and forgot to multiply by the original length

questions.topic: Temperature Scales and Thermal Expansion of Solids, Liquids, and Gases
questions.question: For an isotropic solid, how is the coefficient of superficial (areal) expansion \( \beta \) related to the linear coefficient \( \alpha \)?
questions.explanation:
A square of side \( L \) becomes \( L(1+\alpha\Delta T) \) on each side.

Area becomes \( L^2(1+\alpha\Delta T)^2\approx L^2(1+2\alpha\Delta T) \).

So \( \beta=2\alpha \).
questions.hint: Area involves two lengths, each stretching by the same fraction.
distractor_logic: Swapped the areal ratio with the volume ratio \( \gamma=3\alpha \)
Assumed area expands at the same fractional rate as length
Inverted the relation, as if area expanded more slowly than length

questions.topic: Temperature Scales and Thermal Expansion of Solids, Liquids, and Gases
questions.question: The volume expansion coefficient of a solid is \( \gamma=6\times10^{-5} \) per °C. What is its linear expansion coefficient \( \alpha \)?
questions.explanation:
For an isotropic solid, \( \gamma=3\alpha \).

\( \alpha=\dfrac{\gamma}{3}=\dfrac{6\times10^{-5}}{3}=2\times10^{-5} \) per °C.
questions.hint: Volume involves three lengths.
distractor_logic: Divided by 2, using the areal relation \( \beta=2\alpha \) instead of \( \gamma=3\alpha \)
Multiplied by 3 instead of dividing
Assumed linear and volume coefficients are equal

questions.topic: Temperature Scales and Thermal Expansion of Solids, Liquids, and Gases
questions.question: The temperature of a gas changes by 30 K. What is this change on the Celsius scale?
questions.explanation:
Kelvin and Celsius degrees are the same size, and the 273 offset cancels in a difference.

So \( \Delta T_C=\Delta T_K=30 \) °C.

Subtracted 273 from a temperature difference
Applied the Fahrenheit factor \( \dfrac{9}{5} \), although Kelvin and Celsius degrees are the same size

questions.question: At what temperature does water have its maximum density?
questions.explanation:

questions.question: A black body at 27 °C is heated until it radiates 16 times as much power. What is its new temperature in °C?
questions.explanation:
16 times the power means \( T \) doubles: \( 16^{1/4}=2 \).

300 K becomes 600 K.

In Celsius: \( 600-273=327 \) °C.

questions.question: A black sphere of mass 0.63 kg and surface area \( 0.01\text{ m}^2 \), made of material with specific heat 450 J/(kg·K), is at 1000 K in surroundings near 0 K. At what initial rate does its temperature fall? (\( \sigma=5.67\times10^{-8}\text{ W m}^{-2}\text{ K}^{-4} \))
